questions.stem: The First Governor-General of Bengal (not India) was:
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Warren Hastings was appointed the first Governor of Bengal in 1772 and became the first Governor-General of Bengal (under the Regulating Act 1773) in 1773.

questions.stem: Who was the first Governor-General of India (all India, not just Bengal)?
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833, which unified administration. He abolished sati and suppressed thuggee.

questions.stem: The abolition of sati (1829) is associated with which Governor-General?
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord William Bentinck abolished the practice of sati (self-immolation of widows on their husband's funeral pyre) in 1829, greatly supported by the social reformer Ram Mohan Roy.

questions.stem: The Doctrine of Lapse, which led to the annexation of many Indian princely states, was the policy of:
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse: if a ruler died without a natural male heir, his state was annexed by the British. States so annexed included Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, and Awadh.

questions.stem: The Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793) was introduced by:
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793, fixing land revenue permanently with zamindars. This made zamindars the permanent owners of land but caused exploitation of peasants.

questions.stem: The Indian Universities Act (1904), which gave more government control over universities, was passed during the viceroyalty of:

options.option_text: Lord Curzon — correct, as part of his educational reforms

questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Curzon (1899–1905) passed the Indian Universities Act, 1904 to improve academic standards but it also increased government control and was criticised as an attempt to curb nationalist education.

questions.stem: The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced the principle of:

options.option_text: Separate electorates for Muslims — a major constitutional concession

questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims — Muslims would vote only for Muslim candidates — seen as a divisive policy that deepened communalism.

questions.stem: The partition of Bengal (1905) was ordered by:
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 on administrative grounds but it was widely seen as a divide-and-rule policy. Mass protests and Swadeshi movement followed. The partition was annulled in 1911.

questions.stem: Which Viceroy announced the Communal Award (1932), granting separate electorates to depressed classes (Dalits)?

options.option_text: Lord Willingdon — the Communal Award was by the British Prime Minister MacDonald, during Willingdon's viceroyalty

questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: The Communal Award of August 1932 was announced by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald (not the Viceroy) during Lord Willingdon's viceroyalty. Gandhi fasted against it; it was modified by the Poona Pact.

options.option_text: Passing the Ilbert Bill and local self-government reforms (1882–1883)

questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Ripon (1880–1884) is remembered as a liberal reformer: he introduced local self-government (1882), repealed the vernacular press act, and introduced the controversial Ilbert Bill allowing Indian judges to try Europeans.

questions.stem: The last Viceroy of British India was:
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Louis Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of British India (February–August 1947). He oversaw the transfer of power and the partition of India and Pakistan on 14–15 August 1947.

questions.stem: The Simon Commission (1927), which Indians boycotted for having no Indian members, was sent during the viceroyalty of:

options.option_text: Lord Reading — no, it was Lord Irwin (1926–1931)

questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: The Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928 during Lord Irwin's viceroyalty. Indians boycotted it with 'Simon Go Back' protests because it had no Indian members.

questions.stem: Lord Wellesley is associated with the expansion of British power through which policy?
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: Lord Wellesley (1798–1805) created the Subsidiary Alliance — Indian rulers accepted British troops, paid for their upkeep, and ceded foreign policy — leading to rapid British territorial expansion.

questions.stem: Which Act established 'Dyarchy' — a dual governance system — in Indian provinces?
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: The Government of India Act, 1919 introduced dyarchy in provinces: certain 'transferred' subjects (education, agriculture) went to Indian ministers; 'reserved' subjects (finance, law and order) remained with British governors.

questions.stem: The capital of British India was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in:
questions.subject: History
questions.explanation: The shift of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi was announced at the Delhi Durbar in 1911 by King George V. New Delhi was officially inaugurated in 1931.
